disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to a traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusive memories, dissociation, negative mood, avoidance, and arousal symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month after the trauma, with associated functional impairment. Clinically, ASD often presents with marked distress, sleep and concentration problems, and difficulty resuming normal roles, and it confers elevated risk for later Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) if symptoms persist or intensify. It is distinguished from normal acute stress reactions by symptom severity, breadth of symptom clusters, and significant interference with social or occupational functioning, and from PTSD primarily by its shorter duration and more immediate temporal relationship to the trauma.

narrative.stressor: Ada was driving back from a weekend blues festival in Austin when, on a rural highway after dark, a pickup truck ran a red light and slammed into the passenger side of her car. Although she and the other driver survived with only minor physical injuries, she spent several terrifying minutes trapped in the vehicle, smelling gasoline and listening to the other driver scream until first responders arrived and cut her out. Over the next week, her normally grounding routines—her Red River walking club, her art-therapy volunteering, even planning classes at the university—became increasingly disrupted as she felt unable to get back behind the wheel to commute and found herself breaking down when colleagues mentioned road trips or asked about her weekend. After six days of struggling to get to campus, canceling a book club meeting, and relying on her husband to drive her everywhere, she went to the university counseling center at the urging of a fellow faculty member, worried that her reactions to the crash were "taking over" her life.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since the car accident last week, I keep reliving it over and over in my head, even when I’m trying to work or relax, and I can’t seem to shut it off.”

narrative.stressor: Guillermo was flying back from a high-stakes negotiation on a red-eye flight when the plane hit sudden, extreme turbulence and dropped sharply, causing oxygen masks to deploy and unsecured items to fly through the cabin. For several minutes, passengers screamed and a flight attendant was thrown against the ceiling before the pilots stabilized the aircraft and announced an emergency landing; Guillermo sat strapped in, convinced they were going to crash, mentally rehearsing what would happen to his family and company. In the six days that followed, his usually precise, ordered routine collapsed—he left strategy meetings abruptly, could not bring himself to enter the company’s high-floor conference room with large windows overlooking the Bay, and began avoiding any discussion of upcoming business travel, which was central to his role. After his chief operating officer found him sitting in his office with the door locked, unable to return to a board meeting after hearing a low rumble from a passing truck that reminded him of the plane’s engines, she insisted he see a psychiatrist that same day through the company’s executive health program.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that near-crash on the plane, every small noise or movement makes me jump out of my skin, and I can’t function in meetings because I’m constantly on edge waiting for something bad to happen.”

narrative.stressor: Gloria was at home in Treme cooking gumbo when her husband suddenly collapsed at the kitchen table, gasping for breath and turning blue while she fumbled to remember the 911 operator’s instructions for CPR. The paramedics arrived to find her still pressing on his chest, hands shaking and apron stained, as they took over resuscitation and rushed him to the hospital, where he was stabilized in the intensive care unit after what they described as a "near-fatal" heart attack. Over the next six days, Gloria tried to keep up her routine of organizing quilting circles and attending jazz sets, but she found herself moving mechanically through the community center and then sitting frozen at his bedside in the ICU, barely reacting when friends visited or when staff spoke to her about his condition. When her daughter noticed that Gloria, usually animated and talkative, seemed oddly detached and described feeling like she was "watching someone else’s life" whenever she walked into the hospital, she persuaded her to speak with the hospital’s psychiatry liaison service.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since my husband’s heart attack, it’s like I’m not really here—when I walk into his hospital room, everything feels unreal, like I’m watching it happen to someone else.”
